utterances.text: No, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Perhaps we can play it again and you can just tell us to stop at the moment when you see yourself?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 43.4 and ending at 52 something.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, in fact, you were standing just behind President Milosevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 75 of your statement you say that a lot of Mr. Simatovic's speech sounded, you say: "A lot of it sounded incredible and impossible to me, both then and now." You give a few examples of things that sounded impossible to you and we'll come to those, but before that, I just want to ask you this. In the very next paragraph you say: [As read] "I have never talked with Stanisic about the special operations unit, JSO, or any other unit. In fact, I did not talk about anything else but about the above-mentioned topics regarding international co-operation." Sir, Mr. Simatovic's speech was precisely about this unit that you say you never discussed. According to your own evidence, you have no way of knowing whether Mr. Simatovic's speech was true or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And just because something in Mr. Simatovic's speech sounded unlikely or even impossible to you, that doesn't mean it didn't happen; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be one way of putting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand that answer. My question is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not sure I understood the question either. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think the question in itself is not clear but whether it's a question you can answer, that's a different matter. The problem is combining "unlikely" and "impossible". If I consider something impossible, that can be on grounds which also demonstrate that it cannot be true. If, for example, I say that at 11.00 this day, although I was not outside of this courtroom, that it would be impossible it to be outside being night, then I would think that you could fairly say that this impossibility is of a kind which allows to conclude that it cannot be true. Now, the word "impossible" and "unlikely" are used in various ways. So, therefore, if something is unlikely then that expression in itself already hints at that it's not impossible but not likely that it's true. If you use the word "impossible," you would have to further explore what is the basis for a judgement that something is impossible. Now, sometimes you use the word "impossible" whether it mainly refers to a highly unlikely. In those circumstances of course, you couldn't exclude for the possibility that it nevertheless occurred. So if we want to -- we want to be assisted by the information the witness gives, I think we should further explore what he meant with "unlikely" and "impossible," and by asking further questions that may shed some light on what he said in his statement. Please proceed, Mr. Farr. Mr. Jordash, does this more or less explain -- of course I'm not here to explain the questions of Mr. Farr, but at the same time I think I'm listening to the questions and if I have a certain understanding, I just put it to you to see whether that is the way you understand the question as well. Meanwhile, the witness may then also understand what an ordinary person thinks the question was about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I think I'll just deal with this with specifics.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The first thing that you said sounded incredible or impossible was "a unit command and intelligence team of 5.000 people" and the other thing was 26 training centres. So we'll start with the 5.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And if we could please have the next clip which runs from 14 minutes and 52 seconds to 15 minutes and 18 seconds. That transcript has been marked as "Kula clip 5" for the booths.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "From 12 October 1991, in battles with armed Croatian police forces in the zones of Benkovac, Stari Gospic, Plitvice, Glina, Kostajnica and others, the unit provided important support for the liberation of all areas of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Around 5.000 soldiers were engaged in these battles and their actions were co-ordinated by the unit command and their intelligence team from the 2nd Administration."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, I think that the comment in your statement may be a result of a misunderstanding of what Simatovic said, and that's what I want to address with you. What Mr. Simatovic said was: [As read] "The unit provided important support in the liberation of all areas of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Around 5.000 soldiers were engaged in these battles and their actions were co-ordinated by the unit command and an intelligence team from the 2nd Administration." Now, do you agree with me that Mr. Simatovic did not state that the unit command and intelligence team had 5.000 people, he said that the unit command and intelligence team co-ordinated the actions of 5.000 soldiers? That's what Mr. Simatovic actually said; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I was able to hear, Mr. Simatovic said that there had been co-ordination. 5.000 soldiers does not necessarily mean 5.000 members of our unit. What my understanding of it was 5.000 soldiers overall.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, in fact, those soldiers could have been members of the JNA. They could have been Martic's Police or something else, all of that is possible based on your understanding of what Mr. Simatovic said.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to speculate really. Truly, I don't know the answer to your question. I wasn't familiar with these issues. I merely found this high number illogical.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, just to be clear, I wasn't asking you to confirm that, in fact, members of Martic's Police or the JNA were co-ordinated by members of this unit, just that Mr. Simatovic's speech could be understood that way, that's what he says; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on how a person understands this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to get matters clear. In your statement we read when you say that some sounded incredible and impossible, "for instance, a unit command and intelligence team of 5.000 people." You give that as an example of what you considered to be incredible and/or impossible. The language used in your statement seems to refer to the unit that is command and intelligence consisting of 5.000 people. Now, we've listened to what was said and Mr. Farr has drawn your attention to the fact that 5.000 soldiers would not have necessarily been part of the unit but their action were co-ordinated, and ... Now, the explanation you give now, the 5.000 not necessarily being part of the unit seems to be different from what we read in your statement where at least the language used suggests that your judgement, that it's incredible or impossible is based on 5.000 people in the unit command and/or intelligence. Is my understanding correct that in your statement you may have based your opinion or your judgement on, perhaps, a different understanding of the words spoken than you are giving us now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so. I am a layman where these issues are concerned and I probably interpreted what I heard differently. If that was the case, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's not a matter of apologies. We want to clarify that. Would that also mean that since your attention is now drawn to what those 5.000 soldiers stand for, that the incredibility and the impossibility is not found any more in the number of 5.000 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It still sounds incredible and impossible to me speaking as a layman. Bearing in mind the assets we had at our disposal in Serbia, how would it have been possible for us to maintain and take care of such numbers? I repeat that I'm speaking as a layman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Taking care in this context meaning co-ordinating the activities of 5.000 soldiers? You would say that your assets that were at your disposal would not from a layman's view not allow to co-ordinate the activities of 5.000 soldiers; is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, the second thing that you indicated that you found incredible or impossible was the existence of 26 training camps. And for that I think we need the next clip which runs from 15 minutes 52 seconds to 16 minutes and 19 seconds. Transcripts have been marked for both booths as "Kula clip 6."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Twenty-six training camps for Special Police Units for Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina were also formed in that period. In the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, in Golubic, Dinara, Obrovac, Gracac, Plitvice, Sumarice, Petrova Gora, Licki Osik, Benkovac, Lezimir, Ilok, and Vukovar. And in the RSK, in Banja Luka, Doboj, Samac, Brcko, Bijeljina, Trebinje, Visegrad, Ozren and Mrkonjic Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: We'll now skip slightly ahead to a clip after Mr. Simatovic's speech. This clip begins at 20 minutes and 42 seconds, and it runs to 20 minutes 56 seconds. The transcripts have been marked as "Kula clip 7" for the booths.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "These are the places where we /inaudible/."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, that second clip comes shortly after the end of Mr. Simatovic's speech to the group. In the clip we saw Mr. Stanisic showing something hanging on the wall to Mr. Milosevic and according to the transcript of the video that's been admitted into evidence, we heard Mr. Stanisic say, "these are the places where we," and then the remainder was inaudible to the transcriber. You were in this room in the Kula camp, do you agree with me the object Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Milosevic are looking at is a large metallic map of the former Yugoslavia with numerous locations marked with the wolf symbol of the JSO?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: We'll now switch briefly to a clip from another video. This clip is 65 ter 4787.3. It comes from 65 ter 4787 which is the video with ERN V000-3551. This video contains footage of a press conference held following the JSO's blockade of the Belgrade highway in 2001 and this clip has no dialogue, so there's no transcript. I'll ask Mr. Laugel to start playing the clip and to pause at 20 minutes and 47 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, this video comes from a later period but it appears that we were looking at the same map that Milosevic and Stanisic were looking at in the previous video; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell that it's a map of Yugoslavia, but I can't confirm that it is identical to the other one when it comes to the items marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. I'll now ask Mr. Laugel to keep playing and pause again at 20 minutes and 51 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, the cameraman has apparently zoomed in on a portion of this map. Is this what the map looked like when you had a chance to see it in 1997? Is this the way in which the locations were marked?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell that really. I can't make it out. To tell you the truth, I didn't even examine the map in any detail when I first came to Kula. It was the first visit to Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In the shot we have now, we see several locations marked, including Golubic, Dinara, Obrovac, Gracac and Benkovac. Now, those are all locations mentioned by Mr. Simatovic as locations of training camps in his speech. Does that cause you to change your opinion that the existence of 26 training camps was impossible or incredible?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeated that the opinion I proffered was a layman's -- I misspoke and said logical, it was a layman's opinion and I didn't hear or know anything about the training camps during the visit to Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Are you able to confirm that the wolf's head emblem that we see at each of those locations is the symbol of the JSO?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can yes now continue playing the video and pause again at 21 minutes and 3 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, it appears that the cameraman has now panned north on the map and we see a different group of locations marked. Those include Plitvice and Petrova Gora, among others, which are also locations mentioned by Mr. Simatovic as the locations of training camps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to cut matters short here. Did I understand your testimony well, Mr. Dragicevic, that the 26 camps to be incredible or impossible was not based on any knowledge, just it sounded a lot, is that more or less what your testimony is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right. I did reiterate that it was a layman's opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not based on any specific knowledge about the existence of camps or what the number of camps you would expect to be there, just 26 is a lot and, therefore, I considered it incredible and/or impossible, is that -- please proceed, Mr. Farr, without -- Then we don't have to go through the whole of the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm also looking at the clock at the same time --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to jump to my feet. I was wondering if I might address Your Honours briefly in the absence of the witness concerning an aspect of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time I was looking at the clock. How much time would it take and would Mr. Stanisic prefer to have it done after the break? Or?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I will only be 3 minutes but my learned friend may wish to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then perhaps he takes the break to think about what you are going to address. Mr. Dragicevic, we'll take a break but there's one matter we'll hear first in your absence but if you would like to follow the usher at this moment, I would like to see you back after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The issue is only this: It's about notice. Previously at Your Honours, page transcript 12571 there was an exchange in relation to what the Prosecution's case was as a regards the unit command and the 5.000 men allegedly controlled by the unit command. I asked the Trial Chamber to require the Prosecution to state whether they relied upon that allegation, whether that was a part of the Prosecution case. And in relation to that, Your Honours asked the Prosecution to detail what their case was and the Prosecution stated at transcript 12571 in relation to a question they put to the witness they said this: "Sir, I put it to you that in fact there were at least 5.000 soldiers that were engaged in battles in the fall of 1991 in the Krajina that were supplied weapons by the State Security Service of Serbia." That appeared to be the Prosecution's case at that point in time. Now we've had a series of questions put this witness which appear to demonstrate that they have shifted their position once more and now are suggesting, in fact, there was a unit command in charge of 5.000 men. Now, I don't know what the Prosecution case is now, whether it is that, in fact, 5.000 men were supplied weapons or 5.000 men were controlled by unit command from the DB. So I put it on the record that we don't know what the Prosecution case is in relation to this enormous part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me again tell you how I understood matters, and then to see whether that there was a -- that the unit command and the intelligence of the unit played a role in co-ordinating and, perhaps, supplying material, not necessarily that there was a direct command over those 5.000 soldiers, but I may have misunderstood the evidence and that's the reason why I'm saying it in order to stand corrected, if my understanding is wrong, and I think it's important that the understanding of the Chamber of the evidence is the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- didn't put my point clearly. We -- in short we asked the Prosecution to state whether it was their case that a unit command from the DB had control of 5.000 men in the battles which took place in the RSK in 1991. My learned friend for the Prosecution, Mr. Weber, having been invited to state that, in fact, didn't state that but in fact stated something quite different, that the connection between the DB and the 5.000 men was that the DB had supplied weapons to those 5.000 men. No suggestion at that point that the DB was in control of or co-ordinating those 5.000 men. Supply of weapons was the issue. My concern now is that we seem to have have reverted back to a previous position, i.e., reliance upon the Kula speech by Mr. Simatovic that in fact the 5.000 men were in some way co-ordinated by a unit command from the DB. That's our concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, can you immediately respond or would you rather wait until after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd like to take the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take the break and resume at a quarter to 1.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, any answer to Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this issue has been discussed and litigated before. I think the position is that the case is set out in the indictment in the pre-trial brief. The Chamber has made that observation in its decision and obviously the accused cannot be convicted for anything that is not set out in the indictment. That's the charging instrument. The case is complex by its nature and cannot be put to every single witness, particularly witness who do not have knowledge of a particular aspect. So we would submit that its inappropriate to look at the cross-examination of a single witness to say that the Prosecution didn't put a particular point to the witness and, therefore, conclude that that operates to modify the indictment or the pre-trial brief. The case simply can't be derived from the questioning of a witness. So we would simply reiterate that the case is set out in the indictment and the pre-trial brief and that's been the Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not a very direct answer to Mr. Jordash's question because he wanted to know what exactly was the link between the 5.000 soldiers and the role of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, may I, it wasn't an answer at all to the question, but my learned friend -- there isn't anything in the indictment about a unit command controlling 5.000 men and there's nothing in the pre-trial brief about that so we assume that that is not part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I suggest that everyone reads carefully, you including, Mr. Farr, not to continue a debate on the basis of this answer because that doesn't seem to be -- that will not bear any fruit, but the Chamber, of course, will also consider the matter, we have decided on the matter earlier, not on this specific point, but in more general terms, and we'll give it some thoughts, this exchange between the parties at this moment. Since the witness is not in, I also take the opportunity to give a decision. I take it that the booths have been provided with the text. I already indicate that I will not follow the text exactly in the second part. I made some changes. It is a decision on the Stanisic Defence motion on the admission of two witness statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis. On the 5th of October of this year, the Stanisic Defence filed a motion to add two witnesses to its witness list and to admit their witness statements pursuant to Rule 92 Bis. The motion also requested the admission of evidence of a third witness pursuant to Rule 92 quater. The Chamber will deal with this third witness in a separate decision. On the 19th of October, 2011, the Prosecution responded that it did not oppose adding the two witnesses to the witness list, but requested that they be called for cross-examination. Considering in particular that Prosecution did not oppose the request to add the two witnesses to the witness list, the Chamber grants this part of the motion. The Chamber considers that both witness statements deal with the acts and conduct of the accused and, therefore, denies the request of their admission pursuant to Rule 92 bis. The witness whose statement is contained in Annex B of the motion should be called for cross-examination. The Chamber instructs the Stanisic Defence to schedule this witness and inform the parties and the Chamber of the dates for testimony of this witness by the 14th of November 2011. As for the witness whose statement is contained in Annex A of the motion, the Chamber notes that an important part of his evidence relates to a highly-disputed issue and I'll just shortly summarise this issue. That is, the ability of Mr. Stanisic to perform his official functions during a commission -- during the work of a commission which has been linked several times in the evidence to Mr. Stanisic, and that that evidence in the statement appears to consist of conclusions based on the witness's reading of certain materials, rather than on direct knowledge of facts. In addition, at least some of the material on which the witness relies might be available to the Chamber already. But under these circumstances, the Chamber urges the Stanisic Defence to seriously consider whether it wishes to call the witness, if it expects only to elicit similar conclusions, and on a similar basis, as the ones found in the statement. The Chamber instructs the Stanisic Defence to report its final position whether or not it will call that witness to report to the parties and the Chamber by the 14th of November, 2011. And this concludes the Chamber's decision in this respect. We made it an oral decision also in order to speed up matters. Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If I can just take the opportunity to deal with other witness issues briefly. DST-060 was supposed to be the next witness. He has indicated he doesn't want to come. We are -- and he is adamant about that and we are considering today whether it is going to be at all fruitful to apply for a subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may have noted from the decision of the Chamber that you asked for a subpoena already. We were a bit hesitant because we were not yet sure that he didn't wish to come to The Hague, but that now apparently is clear and which would open the way to a subpoena more easily, whether you want to pursue -- whether you want to insist on calling the witness is, of course, a matter for you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. We'll make a decision today, but given his intransigence, and I use the word carefully, it's not clear that we will apply for a subpoena. But that does then leave the situation somewhat in terms of witnesses for next week somewhat in difficulty. The next witness after that would have been DST-069 who is also subject to a subpoena. Your Honours, will, I think, know the one I'm talking about. But I think given the time-scale, it may be that he or his employers are not able to respond in time to have him here next week. What I'm doing now is having my investigator explore whether in fact, I'm just dealing with this as I think of it, whether in fact the witness, a witness in Annex B might be available for next week instead. That's the situation, we are trying to avoid any loss of court time but dealing with certain difficulties which can largely come about because of DST-060 and his overall unhelpful approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may help, be of assistance to the Chamber to know that should Mr. Jordash apply for subpoena for DST-060, the Prosecution would not oppose it and would defer to the Chamber, should the Chamber advise sufficient grounds had been laid for the issuance of a subpoena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I cannot anticipate on what the decision of the Chamber will be. At the same time, I can assure that if an application for a subpoena will be filed, that the Chamber will, also in view of the fact that the Prosecution has responded that it will not oppose, will deliver its decision at shortest notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I think we will be coming back tomorrow because I think Mr. Farr is travelling some distance and intends to continue travelling, so I would seek to make the application orally tomorrow at the earliest opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then let me just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber commits itself to if a application for a subpoena will be made tomorrow either to decide on the same day or not later than Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Farr, if the witness has returned to the courtroom, you will be ready to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, while he is being brought in I intended to tender the last video shown, 4787.3. That was the video of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No objections? Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4787.3 will receive number P3045, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3045 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Jordash, I received notice that the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Redacted statement of Witness DST-036 has been uploaded and released in e-court but redacted statements are not admitted into evidence, so I think the usual way is to file it, so just for you to know that uploading is fine but that's not the instruction of the Chamber what to do with redacted statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. Should we also file the summary of this witness's evidence rather than read it out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, for the public, the public has not easy access, so if there would be time tomorrow I would still ask you to read it because we want to allow the public to follow the proceedings, rather than to make applications for access to filed documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, you are ready? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just before I begin, I just wanted to confirm that the pseudonym sheet not the pseudonym sheet that the list of names associated with the numbers that the witness has been referring to has been admitted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I must have missed that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not, Madam Registrar will -- we know it was uploaded and I think it was admitted or was it not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's certainly been uploaded. I am not sure it's been admitted. 1D05259.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar will check. If it has not been admitted yet, then the number for the list of names and numbers would be, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was not admitted, Your Honours, so far, so the number for 1D5259 would be D509, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D509 is admitted into evidence under seal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, we'll now return to the Kula video.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we please play the clip now starting with 22 minutes 13 seconds and play through until 22 minutes and 40 seconds. And the transcript of this clip has been marked as "Kula clip 8" for the booths.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "JS: Mr. President, dear guests, let us pay tribute to deputy minister Radovan Stojicic, Badza, by observing a minute of silence. Glory to him." Soldiers: Glory."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, that was you we just saw standing beside Mr. Stanisic in that clip; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And the transcript indicates that it was Mr. Stanisic that called for the minute of silence, is that correct or was it you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: As the protocol co-ordinator of the event, are you able to tell us why there was a minute of silence for Badza?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radovan Stojicic, aka Badza, was deputy minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia and was killed accidently in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: To your knowledge did he have a productive and co-operative relationship with Mr. Stanisic and with the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both sections of the Ministry of the Interior, i.e., the public security and the State Security Services had a very correct co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we now please play the clip beginning with 32 minutes and 24 seconds and ending at 32 minutes 37 seconds and there's no dialogue in this clip so there is no transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, in this clip we just saw Milosevic and Stanisic standing side by side watching television footage. The title on the screen is "Corridor." Are you able to say whether this footage is related to Operation Corridor in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about this because I wasn't part of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Do you know why Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Stanisic were watching that footage together?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we now please have the clip beginning at 33 minutes and 20 seconds and ending at 33 minutes and 57 seconds. And the transcript of this portion has been marked as "Kula clip 9" for the booths.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Apparently there's a technical problem with that clip so we will go on to the next one, which is the clip beginning at 42 minutes and 20 seconds which and the transcript of that one has been marked as "Kula clip 10" for the booths. Now I'm going to ask that this one be paused at 42 minutes and 36 seconds, so we'll start playing at 42 minutes and 20 seconds and pause at 42 minutes and 36 seconds. We can start.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Announcer: To mark the day of the special operations unit of the Republic of Serbia state security, the chief of the Republic of Serbia State Security Service, Mr. Jovica Stanisic, will present awards."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, that is you that has just been speaking on this video; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we continue and pause again at 43 minutes and 18 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Radomir Ratkovic, Sima Ratkovic, Nikola Pupovac, Dragan Olujic."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, we've just seen you announcing names of individuals who then come forward to receive awards from Mr. Stanisic. Is it really your evidence that you never discussed this unit with Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I didn't discuss it with him. As I already said, I had my purview and in this particular instance I was merely acting as a master of ceremony or abiding by the protocol and that was my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we continue playing the clip now through to the end.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Dragan Vasiljkovic. JS: I'm proud to present you with /inaudible/."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, in that clip we just heard you call out the name of Dragan Vasiljkovic, saw him walk forward to accept an award from Jovica Stanisic, hug Jovica Stanisic, and Stanisic then spoke a few words to him. When I asked you earlier today when you met Captain Dragan for the first time, you said that you met him by coincidence in Belgrade several days after the events of 5th October. "He was in the company of a man I knew. That was when we made our acquaintance." That's transcript page 9. Still on transcript page 9 when I asked you, did you ever learn of any link or relationship between Captain Dragan and the Serbian DB, you said no. When I asked you did you ever learn about any links or relationship between Captain Dragan and Jovica Stanisic, you said no. When I asked you as far as you know, did Jovica Stanisic and Captain Dragan ever meet, you said I'm not aware of that. Sir, those answers were not honest, do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said that I met Captain Dragan, I told you the truth. I met him. I used to see him on TV. Now I see after watching this video-clip, because that was a long time ago, I realise that he was there and that he received the award as well. You must admit that after such a long time I had problems remembering everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, it's not just that he happened to be present at the same ceremony where you were present, you called out his name, you were standing about a metre and a half away from him when he received this award, and you are really saying that you forgot that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, all I did was to read the list of the names of those who were the recipients of the award.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: When I asked you whether it was correct that meeting Captain Dragan for the first time was a memorable experience given his fame and notoriety, you said, "Well, I saw images on TV and of course I recognised him right away." Now you are telling us that your first meeting, as you now say, of Captain Dragan is something that you have forgotten, is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what, it probably slipped my mind. There were many people there. I can't tell you right away. I was merely reading the names of those who received the award and you really can't expect me to remember every single name.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to be clear. It's our position that your evidence on this point is not true. You know very well who Captain Dragan is and you know that he was a close associate of Mr. Stanisic, Mr. Simatovic, and the Serbian DB. It's precisely because you know this that you have been dishonest with the court in claiming that you didn't meet him until 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot discuss the level of co-operation between Captain Dragan and Mr. Stanisic and the service in general. I knew nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was a different one. As a matter of fact, what Mr. Farr did put to you is that you didn't tell us the truth for the reasons he mentioned that you knew Captain Dragan well, that you knew that he was a close associate with Mr. Stanisic and Simatovic and the Serbian DB, and that that's what the reason why you didn't tell us the truth. Now, he asked you whether you agree with that or not. I got the impression from your answer that you do not agree, is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Entirely. You understood me perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 84 of your statement, you said: "I know Stanisic very well because I was working with him. I know how he behaves and reacts." Earlier today you told us that in your experience Mr. Stanisic was a man who did not show much emotion whether positive or negative. Can we agree that the hug and handshake that Mr. Stanisic gave to Captain Dragan was, for Mr. Stanisic, an extremely warm demonstration of trust, respect, and affection.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me about things that concern two other individuals. I can only tell you how I would behave under these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, I think that the facts are that what you see on the video is that Mr. Stanisic greets and congratulates Dragan in a way different from the others, that is, I think there will be no dispute about that as a fact. Let's try to avoid to again read the minds and let's focus on the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. To be clear, the only reason I asked the question is because of the witness's representation that he knows how Mr. Stanisic behaves and reacts, but I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if he has any specific knowledge about this specific event, if he has heard anything from Mr. Stanisic why he did it, then of course we could ask him, but let's not try to interpret in any way other than every normal person would be able to interpret certain behaviour and that has to be done with extreme caution and so unless the witness has any specific knowledge on this behaviour at this moment, if not, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we now please have the last clip which runs from 45 minutes 57 seconds to 47 minutes and 13 seconds. The transcripts have been marked as "Kula clip 11".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There, Frenki is correcting our protocol. We have now actually given out the greatest, highest award that can be earned in work of this kind and they are the awards for valour. Each of you that receive this award, be it Opacic in the Knin area or Djurica in the Banija area and even the story about us as men who tried to help their people ... Each one of them is the same, particularly the way it came about, but in essence it speaks of the heroism of our people and what we have put into our unit and who will carry on the tradition of this unit."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir -- first of all, we can agree, I think that is still you standing beside Mr. Stanisic in this clip; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: We just heard Mr. Stanisic say: "Each of you that received this award, be it Opacic in the Knin area or Djurica in the Banija area". Do you know why Mr. Stanisic would have particularly singled out Opacic from the Knin area when he is discussing the people who received the awards for valour?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I've said already that I don't know these men.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to turn back briefly to the take-over of the federal MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we please have P3017 on the screen. This is the report of the police brigade of the federal Ministry of the Interior dated 8 August 1992, compiled by Milorad Davidovic. And if we could focus on the first page on the word "report" and the following few lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, as you can see, this is a report on the engagement of a group of federal MUP police brigade members to provide expert assistance to the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we please have the middle of page 6 in English and the bottom of page 4 in B/C/S. I'm interested in the portion of the document that says: [As read] "The SSUP unit was particularly engaged in the disarming and suppression of the criminal, and in some cases, inhumane activities of certain paramilitary formations in the area." If we could have the next page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: [As read] "The Serbian Volunteer Guard, Captain Dragan's Red Berets, the Yellow Wasps, the police force of the SAO Krajina who were directed to these parts by the Serbian MUP." Sir, earlier in your evidence you told us that you believed that the federal MUP was taken over by the Serbian DB pursuant to an agreement between the ministers. Our position is that this document shows the real reason, which is that Captain Dragan, who we just saw receive an award from Jovica Stanisic, was accused of criminal and in some cases inhumane activity by this report prepared by the federal MUP. That's the real reason for the federal MUP take-over, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not able to answer the question. I did not participate in the take-over of the federal SUP building. Whatever I had to say about it, I said that I had heard and I started to work in the federal SUP building a week or two later perhaps. I am not familiar with what is stated here at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we now please have the bottom half of page 9 in English and the middle of page 7 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'm interested in the portion -- I'm interested in the portion that reads: [As read] "In a well-prepared and organised action that was synchronised with the SRBH MUP and without any human or material losses, all the paramilitary formations in the area of the Bijeljina CSB were disarmed and broken up. The members of these paramilitary formations who had been most deeply involved in criminal activities were arrested and will face criminal prosecution, while the others have been completely disarmed and, after the necessary interviews, returned to the FRY if they were citizens of that country, or assigned to regular units of the army of SRBiH in the case of locals."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And if we could have the next page, please, in English and then continuing below the portion with the three stars in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: [As read] "Information was obtained that in the concluding interviews with members of the paramilitary formations a number of people from these groups categorically stated that they had certain links and contacts with the Republic of Serbia MUP. Zivojin Ivanovic, aka Crnogorac (who was also called Carli and was in Sarajevo for a time) showed an ID card from the Serbian MUP and claimed to be one of its employees, stressing that he and his group had been sent by Tepa and Frenki from the Serbian MUP SDB."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, I'm interested in what this report says about the information contained in the concluding interviews. Isn't it correct that these interviews would have been recorded either in written or some other format, and that the records of those interviews would have been stored in the federal MUP building?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about it. I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, we just saw a man named Zika Ivanovic present the veterans of the special members -- veteran members of the special operation unit of the Republic of Serbia to Jovica Stanisic and Slobodan Milosevic for inspection. This document says that a paramilitary group led by one Zivojin Ivanovic was disarmed and broken up in Bosnia by the federal MUP. And it also indicates that information was gathered linking that group to the Serbian DB. Sir, this is the real reason that the federal MUP building was taken over by the Serbian DB; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to answer the question because I simply don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Okay. I'll turn now to the issue of arrest of Drazen Erdemovic which you discuss in paragraph 61 to 64 of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Turning to the issue of the arrest of Drazen Erdemovic which you discuss in paragraph 61 to 64 of your statement. In paragraph 62 you indicate that you took Erdemovic out of detention and brought him to the DB premises to be heard by the representative of The Hague Tribunal. Were you involved in Erdemovic's initial arrest or did you only become involved at this point?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From that specific point.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter number 6304 on the screen. These are notes of a telephone conversation between Drazen Erdemovic and ICTY investigator Breton Randall. The date is 13 September 2005. If we could have the top of the page and second page in both languages. Is this 65 ter 6304? Sorry, it looks like we don't have the correct document uploaded. I'll just read something to you from the document and ask you whether you are aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In the course of a telephone interview between Drazen Erdemovic and an ICTY investigator on the 13th of September, 2005, the following is recorded: [As read] "He," meaning Erdemovic, "was arrested late at night believed to be the night of 3rd March, 1996, at about 10 or 11.00 hours on Monday, 4 March he was informed by the DB interviewers that he was lucky that his version of events was in the public domain thereby, through inference, affording him some sort of protection from harm as the matter would now have to go before the court. He was interviewed for three days and two nights by the DB. During the course of the interview, the Serbian Ministry of the Interior DB interviewers tried to persuade him to recant his earlier statements to the journalist by now stating that this version of events was wrong because Serbs would never do such a thing, i.e., essentially deny that the events he was involved in at Branjevo and his observations regarding Pilica Dom ever took place." Sir, were you aware of those allegations made by Drazen Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Other than Drazen Erdemovic are you aware of any other arrests related to crimes committed by Serbs at Srebrenica during the time that Jovica Stanisic was head of the DB?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you briefly about some of your comments on the relationship between Milosevic and Stanisic. You say you had the personal impression that Milosevic's attitude towards Stanisic and the DB could best be described as an attitude of mistrust. Now, first of all, we heard you say earlier that Captain Dragan and Jovica Stanisic had no relationship at all and then we just saw evidence that you are aware that they in fact did know each other. On that basis, the Prosecution position is that your evidence regarding the relationship between Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Milosevic is worthless and should not be accorded any weight by this court. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you fully. What was it that I said about Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, you earlier purported to tell us that there was no relationship whatsoever between Jovica Stanisic and Captain Dragan. It's the Prosecution position that that evidence was not honest. On that basis, my suggestion to you is that your evidence regarding the relationship between Jovica Stanisic and Slobodan Milosevic should not be given any weight by this court, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember when it was that I said that there was no sort of relationship between Jovica Stanisic and Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, it was this morning.

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean during the awards ceremony, or, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to cut matters short. Mr. Dragicevic, I think that Mr. Farr is putting the following to you: He says you denied that Captain Dragan had any relation to Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Farr takes the position that he has demonstrated that you are not telling the truth at this moment and he referred in that context to the awards ceremony. Now, he says where it's our position that you didn't tell us the truth in respect of the relationship between Mr. Stanisic and Captain Dragan, whether you would agree with him that the evidence about the relationship between Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Milosevic is useless and not true either? That's, Mr. Farr, what you want to put to the witness. That's what he is putting to you and he would like to hear whether you agree with him or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: You mention a number of things that you say gave you the impression that there was mistrust between Milosevic and Stanisic. One of those things was the relationship between Mr. Stanisic and the American service. You refer to that in terms of the Langley visit in paragraph 72 of your statement, and in terms of a conversation you had with Milosevic at the time Karadzic withdrew from politics. Sir, both of those events, that is the Langley visit and Karadzic's withdrawal from politics happened after the war, so whatever their effect on the relationship between Stanisic and Milosevic was, that effect didn't happen until after the war as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking of the general mistrust that President Milosevic had of the State Security Service which was there right from the start. These were merely two illustrations that I gave, i.e., the official visit to the US and the night when Mr. Stanisic flew over to Mr. Karadzic in order to get from him a signed document certifying that he would no longer be involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: We agree that Stanisic served in the Milosevic government for a long time, seven or eight years; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And he served in a very high-level position, we agree about that as well?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Milosevic could have gotten rid of him any time he wanted to?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right in that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In paragraph 85 of your statement you say: [As read] "I think that Stanisic managed to keep his position as the SDB chief during the period from 1992 until 1998 because Milosevic was smart enough to keep someone on that position who was good in his job. Stanisic was from the DB and had a good team." We can agree on that basis that whatever their subjective feelings for each other, Milosevic and Stanisic worked together professionally and effectively; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that Mr. Milosevic was intelligent enough to keep by his side a man who was a proven professional and who liked his job very much. Why would he have gotten rid of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In other words, Milosevic appreciated and valued Stanisic's work?

utterances.speaker: VLADO DRAGICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you view it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, I'm looking at the clock. Before we adjourn, could you inform the Chamber how much more time you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Probably 15 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 15 minutes. Then you'll have 15 minutes tomorrow. Mr. Dragicevic, we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom, and I give you the same instruction as I did yesterday, that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given tomorrow, and we'll expect to conclude your testimony tomorrow. We stand adjourned and we resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 10th of November, 9.00. Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 10th day of November, 2011 at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.
